Categories.value: Daniel Havell|Munger Fort|Artworks without Wikidata item|PD-old-100-expired|PD-Art (PD-old-100-expired)|Artworks with known accession number|CC-PD-Mark|British Library Asia, Pacific and Africa Collections|Twenty-four Views by Henry Salt (1809)

Artist.value: Daniel Havell / After Henry Salt

ImageDescription.value:
"A View within the Fort of Monghyr" from  'Twenty Four Views in St. Helena, the Cape, India, Ceylon, the Red Sea, Abyssinia and Egypt'.
This aquatint is taken from plate 4 of Henry Salt's 'Twenty Four Views in St. Helena, the Cape, India, Ceylon, the Red Sea, Abyssinia and Egypt'. Situated near Bengal, the fort at Monghyr was strategically important. The Mughal minister Raja Todar Mal occupied it while quelling Bengali rebel forces. It later hosted the Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb's brother, Shuja, during the struggle between the brothers for power. Mir Qasim Ali, the Nawab of Bengal, then used it as a base in his battle against the British. When Mir Qasim was defeated in 1764 the fort lost its importance, and by the time of this image the ancient town of Monghyr was full of convalescing sepoys (soldiers). The Governor General, Lord Cornwallis, had a country house in Monghyr. Now called Munger, it is in the state of Bihar.

Artist.value: William Hodges

ImageDescription.value:
The East End of the Fort of Mongheer view 2.
This is plate 30 from William Hodges' book, 'Select Views in India'. Hodges compared the east view of the fort of Monghyr to an English castle; its impressive structure protected by a deep ditch. He wrote: "This view shows the great care that has been taken to make this fortress formidable. A ditch ... surrounded the land side, and communicated to the river at either extremity, most perfectly insulating it. From neglect it is now dry, there not being the same necessity in our times, from the various stations of troops in the country."

ImageDescription.value:
Fort at Monghyr on the river Ganges, India. Coloured etching by William Hodges, 1787.
This is plate 29 from William Hodges' book, 'Select Views in India'. Hodges went to Monghyr in 1781 to draw the fort, which was under British control at that time. Monghyr was a place of considerable importance for the British in Bengal. It was previously an important military outpost for the Mughals, and the fort had been substantially extended by them. The fort is an impressive structure with three gates, one of which had been a strong fortification with square towers, with a deep ditch to protect the landward approach.

pages.title: File:Munger Fort, Bihar.jpg

ObjectName.value: Munger Fort, Bihar

Categories.value: Munger Fort|Self-published work|Images from Wiki Loves Monuments 2022 in India|Indian monuments with Wikidata QIDs|Files with coordinates missing SDC location of creation|India photographs taken on 2021-09-19|Files from competitions organized by West Bengal Wikimedians User Group|Uploaded via Campaign:wlm-in-br|Images from Wiki Loves Monuments 2022|Images from WLM 2022 India under review by Montage tool

ImageDescription.value:
This fort is one of the most important monuments at Munger. It was built on a rocky eminence projecting into the river Ganges that protects it from west and partly from the north, the other side’s being defended by a deep moat.

The history of this Mungar fort is of around 1330. It is said that the Muslim emperors of India took the construction of this fort in their own hands and completed it in the 14th century itself.

Its history is not completely dated but it is believed that it was built during the early rule of Slave dynasty of India. The Munger town where the fort is situated was under the control of Muhammad bin Tughluq of Delhi (1325-1351).
